title: Exceptions
html:
throw signals an error that the current function can't handle; the stack unwinds (destroying locals) until a matching catch is found.

throw / try / catch

Rule

Throw by value, catch by const reference (catch (const std::exception& e)). Catching by value copies and slices derived exceptions; catching by reference keeps their dynamic type and what().

The standard hierarchy

ExceptionThrown by / used for
std::exceptionBase of all — has virtual const char* what()
std::logic_error → invalid_argument, out_of_range, length_error, domain_errorBugs detectable before running: bad arguments, vector::at, stoi
std::runtime_error → range_error, overflow_error, system_errorErrors only detectable at run time: I/O, OS
std::bad_allocnew failed
std::bad_cast, std::bad_optional_access, std::bad_variant_access, std::bad_function_callMisused library types

Custom exceptions & rethrowing

Stack unwinding

Do

Use exceptions for exceptional failures that the immediate caller can't sensibly handle (I/O failure, invalid config, out of memory). Rely on RAII so unwinding cleans up.

Avoid

Using exceptions for normal control flow (e.g. “not found” in a lookup), throwing from destructors, or catch (...) {} that silently swallows errors.

Watch out

If an exception escapes main (or any noexcept function), std::terminate is called and the program aborts — destructors of the remaining stack may not run.

What happens when an exception is thrown?

The exception object is copied/moved into special storage, then the runtime searches up the call stack for a matching catch. Each frame it leaves is unwound: local objects are destroyed in reverse order. When a handler matches (by type, allowing derived-to-base), it runs; if none matches, std::terminate is called.

Exceptions vs error codes?

Exceptions can't be ignored silently, separate the error path from the happy path, and carry rich information through many layers. Error codes (or std::optional/std::expected) are explicit in the signature, cheaper when failure is common, and required where exceptions are disabled (some embedded/game code). Many code bases use exceptions for rare failures and return values for expected ones.
